input.idea: ChatGPT Plus vs Claude Pro: which one is more useful for a programmer? Both cost about $20 a month, so the question is what you actually get for coding. Compare them on real dev work: writing and fixing code, understanding a large codebase, working in the terminal (Claude Code vs Codex), usage limits during a long coding session, and extras like image generation or voice. End with a clear verdict: who should pick which one.

template.reason: Your idea asks one clear question: which $20 plan is better for coding? This template answers a question step by step, so each step can be one round (writing and fixing code, large codebases, Claude Code vs Codex, usage limits, extras), and the final answer is your verdict. None of the templates is built for comparing two products, though, and this one tops out around 70 seconds, so you'll need to keep each round short to stay near 90.

hooks.text: ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro: which $20 actually codes better?
So, you want the best $20 AI subscription for coding...
Could this be the AI that finally beats ChatGPT for programmers?

hook.text: ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro: which $20 actually codes better?

research.facts:
- Both plans cost $20 a month, and both now come with a terminal coding agent: Claude Pro includes Claude Code, and ChatGPT Plus includes Codex. Each one runs in your terminal and in IDEs like VS Code.
- Claude Pro has a 5-hour session limit plus a weekly limit. Claude Code and the regular Claude chat use the same allowance, so time spent chatting leaves less for coding.
- Codex on ChatGPT Plus also uses 5-hour windows, and weekly limits "may also apply." OpenAI estimates about 15–160 local messages every 5 hours on GPT-6.1 Sol, and up to 3,000 on the lighter GPT-6 Luna model. Cloud tasks use up the allowance faster.
- If you hit the cap partway through a long session, either plan lets you keep going by paying for extra credits. On Claude, extra usage is billed at standard API rates. You can also upgrade to the next plan: Claude Max or ChatGPT Pro.
- Extras: ChatGPT Plus can create images and has voice with video. Claude only writes text and can't create images, though it can read images you upload. Claude does have a voice mode on every plan.
- Usage numbers are estimates and change often. Both companies tell you to check your live usage dashboard; in Claude Code, that's the /status command.

scenes.voiceover: So the real difference isn't just the agent. It's what happens three hours into a long coding session: the usage limits.
scenes.onScreen: The real difference: usage limits
scenes.visual: A clock speeds forward from 0h to 3h beside a code editor, and a battery-style usage bar drains toward red

scenes.voiceover: Second, Codex on ChatGPT Plus. Also five-hour windows, and weekly limits may apply. OpenAI estimates fifteen to a hundred sixty local messages per window on GPT-6.1 Sol.

scenes.voiceover: Switch to the lighter GPT-6 Luna model, and that goes up to three thousand. But cloud tasks use up the allowance faster.
scenes.onScreen:
GPT-6 Luna: up to 3,000
Cloud tasks drain faster

scenes.voiceover: Hit the cap halfway through? Both let you keep going with extra credits. On Claude, that's billed at standard API rates. Or upgrade to Claude Max or ChatGPT Pro.

scenes.visual: Usage bar hits 100% with a red "LIMIT" stamp; two exits fork from it: a coin stack labeled "Extra credits (API rates on Claude)" and an up-arrow to "Claude Max / ChatGPT Pro"

scenes.onScreen:
Images + marathons → ChatGPT Plus
Claude Code, little chat → Claude Pro
scenes.visual: Decision flowchart: two branches end on the ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro logos, each lighting up as its line is spoken

prompt.system:
You are the producer of a short-video channel (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).
Your job in this step: choose how the video will be told, by picking ONE template
from the list you are given. You do not write the video yet.

You get the channel, the video idea and the templates.
Pick the template whose "when to use" fits the idea best; the length matters less.
A template's "needs" are the facts its required scenes are built on. Pick one the idea
can fill with its OWN facts: a rise-to-success story needs a success to show, a how-to
needs steps, a list needs items. If the idea lacks what a template needs, that template
does not fit, however close its topic is.
Never invent a template: answer only with an id from the list.
score: 5 = made for this idea and the idea has every fact it needs, 3 = workable,
1 = nothing in the list fits.
reason: one or two sentences for the creator, in plain English, about this idea.

Templates:
- id: analogy-explainer
  name: Explained with characters
  what: A concept explained through a small invented world or everyday analogy
  when to use: An idea that is an abstract concept (economics, health, finance) that becomes clear as a story.
  needs: problem, step, concept-term, real-case, lesson
  length: 26–63 s
- id: app-list
  name: Free apps list
  what: A quick list of apps, one per scene, each shown on screen
  when to use: An idea that recommends several apps or tools for one device or audience.
  needs: app-count, device-or-audience, app-name, app-feature
  length: 14–62 s
- id: brand-origin
  name: Rise of a brand
  what: From a humble start, through hardship, to a big brand
  when to use: An idea that is the history of a brand, product or founder that has already grown big: the idea gives the success to show (users, money, years). Not a creator telling why they built their own tool.
  needs: year-or-result, brand, founder, start, hardship, time-jump, result-number
  length: 43–80 s
- id: build-it-fast
  name: Build it fast
  what: Show the finished thing, then every step that built it
  when to use: An idea where the viewer can build something real in minutes with a tool.
  needs: result, time, tool-name, step, screen-recording
  length: 20–51 s
- id: dark-true-story
  name: Creepy true story
  what: A dark or strange true story told step by step to a shocking ending
  when to use: An idea that is a real crime, legend or eerie event.
  needs: place-or-person, event, ending
  length: 15–51 s
- id: explained-in-time
  name: Explained in 60 seconds
  what: A complex topic explained in a promised short time, often to an unlikely audience
  when to use: An idea that is a complex topic the viewer finds hard and wants explained quickly.
  needs: nothing special
  length: 35–54 s
- id: how-to-steps
  name: How-to steps
  what: A how-to promise followed by numbered steps on screen
  when to use: An idea that is a concrete task the viewer wants to do with a tool, in a few steps.
  needs: task, tool-name
  length: 32–43 s
- id: myth-vs-reality
  name: Myth vs reality
  what: What people think, then how it really works, with the proof
  when to use: An idea that corrects a common belief or reveals a hidden side of something familiar.
  needs: belief, background, reality, step, twist
  length: 26–59 s
- id: new-tool-news
  name: New tool news
  what: A just-released free tool, its benefits, a quick demo and a comment-keyword offer
  when to use: An idea that is news about a newly released or newly free tool.
  needs: who-released, tool-name, benefit, keyword, resource
  length: 30–107 s
- id: pain-to-fix
  name: Problem then fix
  what: The broken or painful way first, then the tool that fixes it, shown working
  when to use: An idea where a tool fixes a pain the audience recognises, including a creator telling why they built their own tool: the pain they had, then the tool that fixes it.
  needs: pain, task, screen-recording
  length: 30–40 s
- id: plot-recap
  name: Story recap
  what: A plot, journey or character backstory retold event by event
  when to use: An idea that recaps an episode, myth, game lore or a character's story.
  needs: story-name, setting, ending
  length: 48–181 s
- id: product-promo
  name: Product promo
  what: A product's benefits shown one by one through its interface, ending on where to get it
  when to use: An idea that promotes one product or service.
  needs: product-name
  length: 11–30 s
- id: question-answered
  name: Big question answered
  what: A why or how question, answered step by step with diagrams
  when to use: An idea that is a question the audience has wondered about.
  needs: question
  length: 43–71 s
- id: ranked-countdown
  name: Top N countdown
  what: Ranked items counted down to number one
  when to use: An idea that ranks a set of things by some measure.
  needs: rank-count, ranked-thing, rank-number, item-name, item-detail
  length: 25–60 s
- id: rapid-facts
  name: Rapid-fire facts
  what: Many short facts in a row, one per scene, with the strongest kept for last
  when to use: An idea that is a collection of short surprising facts around one theme.
  needs: theme, fact
  length: 40–56 s
- id: single-fact
  name: One surprising fact
  what: One fact built up line by line to a short reveal
  when to use: An idea that is a single surprising or eerie fact that fits in under 20 seconds.
  needs: topic
  length: 7–16 s
- id: software-tutorial
  name: Software how-to
  what: A finished result first, then the steps to make it in the software
  when to use: An idea that is a specific thing to make in a common program (PowerPoint, GitHub, a no-code tool).
  needs: result, software
  length: 14–53 s
- id: tool-deep-dive
  name: Tool explained
  what: What a tool is, how it differs, and what it really does
  when to use: An idea that explains one popular tool or model and how to think about it.
  needs: tool-name, difference, main-point
  length: 49–78 s
- id: tool-spotlight
  name: Tool spotlight
  what: One website or tool shown working, often as a numbered series part
  when to use: An idea that is a single useful website, repo or tool the viewer probably has not seen.
  needs: tool-category, series-part, screen-recording
  length: 10–56 s
- id: tool-tips-keyword
  name: Tool tips list
  what: Numbered tips for one tool, each named and then shown working, ending with a comment-keyword offer
  when to use: An idea that is a handful of concrete tips, skills or add-ons for one tool the audience already uses.
  needs: tool-name, tip-count, tip-number, tip-name, keyword, resource
  length: 47–88 s

  type: question

prompt.system:
You write the script of a short vertical video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts).

Tell ONE connected story. The idea may be written as loose thoughts in any order: sort
them into the order the template's scenes tell (the problem before the fix, the cause
before the result), and let every scene follow from the one before it – the voiceovers
read in a row must make sense as one spoken text. A scene that promises something ("what I learned", "here's why") is
followed by the scene that says it.

The template is a guide: a structure that has worked for videos like this – its scenes,
their order and how they link. Follow it where it serves this idea; change the order,
leave a scene out or add one when that tells this story better. A "repeatable" scene
may appear several times in a row (one per step or item). Put every template scene you
leave out in "skipped" with a short reason.
A scene's "facts" come from the idea and the facts found online only – never invent a
tool, a number or a result.
When the idea has no fact for a scene, leave it out if it is optional; if it is required,
fill it with what the idea does say rather than with an invented claim.
Its "creative" parts are yours to word.

The first scene is the hook: say the chosen hook as it is, and show its key words.
The template's links ("→ next") and the transition phrases are examples of how scenes
can follow each other; use them only where they read naturally. End the way that fits
this video best: the CTA formulas show endings that have worked – use one, or write
your own, or none if no ending asks for one.
The call to action never sends people to a link, a website, a download or a giveaway
the idea does not mention – then pick a CTA formula that needs none of those.

For every scene:
- voiceover: what is said, natural spoken English
- onScreen: the key words shown big, not the whole sentence
- visual: what the viewer sees, concrete (a terminal running a command, a settings page,
  an app icon), never "something engaging"
- needsRecording: your call – true when the scene is shown best with the creator's own
  screen recording rather than a picture the video editor draws.

Keep within the limits. Each scene lasts about as long as its voiceover: fill the wanted
length – add more steps or items with the repeatable scenes, keep the optional scenes
that help – rather than stopping short.

Hook: ChatGPT Plus or Claude Pro: which $20 actually codes better?

Template: Big question answered – A why or how question, answered step by step with diagrams
Scenes:
- opening / hook (1.5–5.5 s): Asks the question. [required] → next: question-answer; facts: question
- opening / setup (3–7 s): Gives the first piece of the answer. [optional] → next: sequence; facts: starting-fact
- build / setup (3–7 s): Lays out the background. [optional] → next: sequence; facts: background
- build / problem (4.7–8.2 s): Names the problem behind the question. [optional] → next: cause-effect; facts: problem
- build / mechanism (4–9.6 s): Explains how it works, one step per scene. [optional] [repeatable] → next: sequence; facts: step
- core / mechanism (4–9.6 s): Continues the explanation to the key point. [optional] [repeatable] → next: cause-effect; facts: step
- core / item (5–6.4 s): Names one stage or part. [optional] [repeatable] → next: example; facts: stage
- climax / problem (4.7–8.2 s): Shows the escalating consequences. [optional] → next: escalation; facts: consequence
- close / payoff (5.4–7 s): Wraps the answer in one line. [optional] → next: none; creative: answer-line
- close / cta (3.2–4.8 s): Asks what to explain next. [optional] → next: none; creative: question

Transition phrases:
- sequence: First, | Second, | Third, | First is | Second is | Third is
- cause-effect: So | As a result | And since | In other words, | You see, | And look
- escalation: And it gets even better | But that's not all. | Plus | Plus, you still get | and here you get | that lets you
- example: Here's another example | They say | Anytime | In many cases, | That's like | You can see
- question-answer: The answer is | It's because of | Well, | But how do | Did you know | So where did the ROAD part come from?

CTA formulas (types allowed: none, question):
- question: Which [item] is your favourite? Tell us in the comments. (e.g. "Drop a comment and tell us which singer is your favorite and which of their songs was your favorite.")
- question: What should I explain next? Leave an idea in the comments. (e.g. "What should I explain next? Leave an idea in the comments")
- question: Do you like [topic] too? Tell me in the comments. (e.g. "Do you like dosa too? Comment mein batayein.")

Limits, from the analysis of successful videos:
- speak at most 3.4 words per second
- a scene lasts at most 9 s, the hook at most 5 s
- at most 15 words on screen in a scene

prompt.system:
You turn the approved script of a short vertical motion video into pictures.
Every frame shows a stage: big pictures (blocks) and the spoken words, which the code
draws from the voiceover by itself.

For every scene, decide which stage tells it best – your call, from what the scene says
and what comes before and after it.
Then pick 1–4 blocks from the catalogue and fill them (none for a statement):
- onWord: the word of THAT scene's voiceover on which the block appears; the blocks go in
  the order their words are said
- the first block appears on the scene's first or second word
- a new block at least every 3 seconds – about every 8 spoken words; one picture standing
  longer feels slow
- the block shows what is being said at that moment, concretely: the tool that is named,
  the command, the number, the steps – never a decoration
- fill exactly the fields the catalogue gives that block
- keywords: 1–4 words of the voiceover to stand out in the spoken text (the names, the
  numbers, the one word that carries the scene)

Use only the logo and prop ids given. When you want a logo or an object that is not
there, show the scene with another block and write what you wanted in wishes (e.g.
"Notion logo"). Answer with one entry per scene, in the same order.
prompt.user:
Channel: TikMaker and AI coding. Mostly TikMaker itself: what it can do, how a video gets made with it, new features and how it is being built with AI (build in public). Around that, short concrete videos about other AI tools, vibe coding and Claude Code: one problem or one feature per video, shown on screen rather than told.
Idea: ChatGPT Plus vs Claude Pro: which one is more useful for a programmer? Both cost about $20 a month, so the question is what you actually get for coding. Compare them on real dev work: writing and fixing code, understanding a large codebase, working in the terminal (Claude Code vs Codex), usage limits during a long coding session, and extras like image generation or voice. End with a clear verdict: who should pick which one.

Stages:
- top: one picture above, the spoken words below
- bottom: the spoken words above, one picture below
- statement: no picture – only the spoken words, big, over the whole frame; blocks: []
- full: one picture over the whole frame, the spoken words over it
- split: two pictures at once, one above the other, the spoken words below; at least 2 blocks

Blocks:
- logos: ids: 2–4 logo or prop ids – when tools, apps or companies are named
- code: file, lines: 2–6 lines of code, at most 35 characters each; start the key line with "+ " – when the scene is about code or a setting
- terminal: lines: the command first, then 1–2 lines of its output – when the scene is about a command
- list: items: 2–4 short points, at most 24 characters each – benefits, steps, mistakes
- number: value, prefix (e.g. $), suffix (e.g. %, k), text: what the number means – a price, a time, a percentage
- compare: before and after: { label, value }, e.g. "Official price" "$49/mo" → "With TikMaker" "$0.016" – before / after, expensive / cheap
- badge: text: "01" or two words – a new point in a numbered list
- object: id: one prop id – a metaphor or a feeling (a padlock, a clock, a robot)
- schema: nodes: 2–4 { label, id? } – how something works, A → B → C
